title: The Story of Merlin: Chapter 1
paragraphs: _This is an account of how Merlin was enchanted by a damsel named Vivien, and of everything that followed from it._
_It also tells how King Arthur was betrayed by his own sister, and how he would surely have been killed if not for the help of Vivien, the same enchantress who caused Merlin’s ruin._
_And it tells how the sheath of Excalibur was lost at that time._
_How Queen Morgana le Fay Plotted Evil Against King Arthur and Sent a Damsel to Trick the Enchanter Merlin._

Now Morgana le Fay was a very cunning enchantress. She was so skilled in magic that her powerful spells could bend all things to her will, whether living or dead. Merlin himself had once been her teacher. He had taught her his arts when she was still a young damsel at the Court of Uther-Pendragon. So, next to Merlin, she was at that time the most powerful enchanter in all the world. Still, she did not have Merlin’s foreknowledge of things to come, or his gift of prophecy. Merlin could not pass these gifts on to anyone, and so she had never learned them from him.

Now, after Queen Morgana le Fay had come to the Island of Avalon, as was told before, she brooded for a long time over the insult that she believed King Arthur had done to her house. The more she brooded, the bigger it grew in her mind. At last it seemed to her that she could have no joy in life unless she punished King Arthur for what he had done. Indeed, she would have been glad to see him dead at her feet, so great was her anger against him.

But Queen Morgana knew very well that she could never harm the King, her brother, while Merlin was there to protect him. Merlin would surely foresee any danger that threatened the King, and he would defeat it. So she knew that if she wanted to destroy the King, she must first destroy Merlin.

Now, at the Court of Queen Morgana le Fay there was a certain damsel whose beauty was so marvelous and bewitching that hardly her equal could be found in all the world. This damsel was fifteen years old and of royal blood, for she was the daughter of the King of Northumberland. Her name was Vivien. Vivien was wise and cunning beyond measure for one so young. She was also without any heart, and she was cold and cruel to anyone who stood against her wishes. Because she was so cunning and wise, Queen Morgana liked her and taught her many of the secrets of magic and sorcery that she knew. But in spite of all that Queen Morgana did for her, the girl felt no love for her mistress, for she had no heart at all.

One day this damsel and Queen Morgana le Fay sat together in a garden on the magic island of Avalon. The garden lay on a very high terrace and looked out over the sea. The day was very fair, and the sea was so wonderfully blue that it seemed as if the blue sky had melted into water and the water into sky. As Vivien and the Queen sat in this lovely place, the Queen said to the damsel, “Vivien, what would you rather have than anything else in all the world?” Vivien answered, “Lady, I would rather have wisdom like yours than anything else.”
Then Queen Morgana laughed and said, “You can be as wise as I am, and even wiser, if you will do as I direct you. For I know a way for you to gain wisdom.”
“How can I gain that wisdom, Lady?” asked Vivien.

Then Queen Morgana le Fay said, “Listen, and I will tell you. You must know that Merlin, whom you have seen several times at the Court of King Arthur, is master of all the wisdom that anyone can possess in this world. Everything I know of magic, Merlin has taught me. But he knows many things that he did not teach me, and he kept them back from me. Merlin taught me when I was a young damsel at the Court of my mother’s husband, because he found me beautiful. Merlin loves beauty above all other things in the world, and so he taught me many things of magic and was very patient with me.
“But Merlin has a gift that belongs to him alone and that he cannot give to anyone else, for it is born in him. That gift is the power of seeing into the future and of foretelling what will happen.
“Yet although he can foresee the fate of others, he is blind to his own. He admitted this to me several times: he cannot tell what will happen in his own life when it concerns only himself.

“Now you, Vivien, are far more beautiful than I was at your age. So I believe you will easily win Merlin’s favor. And if I also give you a certain charm that I own, I may make Merlin love you so much that he will share with you far more of his wisdom than he ever taught me when I was his pupil.

“But you must know, Vivien, that in winning this knowledge from Merlin you will put yourself in great danger. In time, when the charm of your beauty has faded for him, he may easily regret that he shared his wisdom with you. Then there will be great danger that he will cast a spell on you to take away your powers. For it would be impossible for both of you to live in the same world, each knowing so much of the cunning arts of magic.”

Vivien listened to all of this very closely. When Queen Morgana had finished, the damsel said, “Dear Lady, everything you tell me is very wonderful, and I feel a burning desire to gain such knowledge of magic. If you will help me in this, so that I may draw his wisdom out of Merlin, I will owe you a debt for as long as I live. As for any danger that may come to me, I am quite willing to take it on. I have great hope that I can protect myself from Merlin so that no harm will come to me. When I have drawn out all the knowledge I can from him, I will use that same knowledge to cast such a spell on him that he will never be able to harm me or anyone else again. In this I will match my wit against his wisdom and my beauty against his cunning, and I believe I will win the game.”

Then Queen Morgana burst into laughter beyond all measure. When she had stopped laughing, she cried, “Ha, Vivien! Truly you are more cunning than anyone I ever heard of, and I believe you are as wicked as you are cunning. For who ever heard of a child of fifteen years who would speak such words as you have just spoken? Who could imagine that so young a girl could think of bringing down the wisest magician who ever lived?”

Then Queen Morgana le Fay put a small whistle of ivory and gold to her lips and blew very shrilly upon it. In answer, a young page of her Court came running. Queen Morgana commanded him to bring her a certain alabaster casket, cunningly carved, decorated with gold, and set with several precious stones. She opened the box and took out two rings of pure yellow gold, beautifully made and set. One ring held a clear white stone of extraordinary brilliance, and the other held a stone as red as blood. Then Queen Morgana said, “Vivien, look at these two rings! Each one holds a spell of wonderful power. If you wear the ring with the white stone, whoever wears the ring with the red stone will love you with such a passion that you can make him do whatever you wish. So take these rings and go to King Arthur’s Court, and use them as your cunning sees fit.”
So Vivien took the two rings and thanked Queen Morgana le Fay again and again for them.

Now King Arthur took great pleasure in holding a grand feast every Pentecost, when his Court gathered around him with much joy and laughter. At such times he loved to have good entertainment to amuse himself and his Court, and so it happened that almost always something occurred that gave the King great delight. So the Feast of Pentecost came, and King Arthur sat at the table with a great many noble and lordly people and several kings and queens. As they all sat at the feast, their spirits lifted by merriment and good cheer, a very beautiful young damsel suddenly came into the hall. With her came a dwarf, wonderfully misshapen and hideous to look at. The maiden was dressed entirely in flame-colored satin, very rich, with beautiful embroidery of gold and silver. Her hair, which was red like gold, was coiled in a net of gold. Her eyes were black as coals and extraordinarily bright and glistening. Around her throat she wore a gold necklace of three strands. With all that gold and those bright clothes, she shone with wonderful splendor as she entered the hall. The dwarf who came with her was also dressed all in flame-colored clothing. In his hands he carried a cushion of flame-colored silk with tassels of gold, and on the cushion lay a ring of exceeding beauty set with a red stone.
When King Arthur saw this beautiful maiden, he thought it was nothing other than some fine entertainment, and he was very glad of it.

But when he looked at the damsel closely, her face seemed familiar to him. So he said to her, “Damsel, who are you?” “Sir,” she said, “I am the daughter of the King of Northumberland, and my name is Vivien.” At that, King Arthur was satisfied.

Then King Arthur said to her, “Lady, what is that on the cushion there, and why have you honored us by coming here?” Vivien answered, “My lord, I have here a very good entertainment to give you pleasure at this Feast of Pentecost. This is a ring of such a kind that only the wisest and most worthy of all the men here may wear it.” And King Arthur said, “Let us see the ring.”

So Vivien took the ring from the cushion that the dwarf held and brought it to King Arthur, and the King took it into his own hand. He saw that the ring was extraordinarily beautiful, and he said, “Maiden, may I try this ring on my finger?” And Vivien said, “Yes, my lord.”
So King Arthur tried to put the ring on his finger, but, behold, the ring shrank so that it would not go past the first joint. So King Arthur said, “It seems that I am not worthy to wear this ring.”

Then the damsel Vivien said, “Have I my lord’s leave to offer this ring to others of his Court?” And King Arthur said, “Let the others try the ring.” So Vivien carried the ring to the various people of the Court, both lords and ladies, but not one of them could wear it. Last of all, Vivien came to the place where Merlin sat. She knelt on the ground before him and offered him the ring. Because this concerned himself, Merlin could not look into the future to see that harm was meant for him. Even so, he looked sourly at the damsel and said, “Child, what is this silly trick you offer me?” “Sir,” said Vivien, “I beg you to try this ring on your finger.” Then Merlin looked at the damsel more closely, and he saw that she was very beautiful, and his heart softened toward her a great deal. So he spoke more gently to her and said, “Why should I take the ring?” She answered, “Because I believe you are the wisest and most worthy of any man in this place, and so the ring should belong to you.” Then Merlin smiled, and he took the ring and put it on his finger, and, behold, it fitted the finger exactly. Then Vivien cried out, “See! The ring fits his finger, and he is the wisest and most worthy!” And Merlin was greatly pleased that the ring the beautiful damsel had given him fitted his finger in that way.

Then, after a while, he wanted to take the ring off again, but, behold, he could not. The ring had grown onto his finger as if it were a part of the flesh and bone. At this Merlin became troubled in spirit and very anxious, for he did not understand what the magic of the ring might mean. So he said, “Lady, where did this ring come from?” And Vivien said, “Sir, you know all things. Do you not know, then, that this ring was sent here from Morgana le Fay?” Then Merlin was greatly in doubt again, and he said, “I hope there is no evil in this ring.” And Vivien smiled at him and said, “What evil could there be in it?”

By this time the great magic in the ring began to work upon Merlin’s spirit. He looked at Vivien steadily, and suddenly he took great pleasure in her beauty. Then the magic of the ring took full hold of him, and, behold, a wonderful passion seized his heart at once and wrung it until it was pierced as with violent pain.

And Vivien saw what was passing in Merlin’s mind, and she laughed and turned away. Several others who were there also noticed the very strange way that Merlin looked at her, and they said among themselves, “Surely Merlin is bewitched by the beauty of that young damsel.”

So, from that time on, the enchantment of the ring of Morgana le Fay worked so upon Merlin’s spirit that he could in no way free himself from Vivien’s witchery. From that day forth, wherever she went, he could be found not far away. If she was in the garden, he was there. If she was in the Hall, he was there also. If she went hawking, he rode along on horseback. All the Court observed these things, and many made merry and joked about it. But Vivien hated Merlin with all her might, for she saw that everyone laughed at Merlin’s folly, and his attention wearied her. But she hid her dislike when she was in front of him, and she behaved toward him in every way as though she had a great friendship for him.

Now it happened one day that Vivien sat in the garden. The summer weather was wonderfully pleasant, and Merlin came into the garden and saw Vivien where she sat. But when Vivien saw Merlin coming, she suddenly felt so great a dislike for him that she could not bear to be near him at that moment. So she rose in haste, meaning to escape from him. But Merlin hurried and caught up with her, and he said to her, “Child, do you hate me, then?” And Vivien said, “Sir, I do not hate you.” But Merlin said, “In very truth, I believe that you do hate me.” And Vivien was silent.

Then, after a little while, Merlin said, “I wish I knew what I could do for you so that you would stop hating me, for I find that I have a wonderful love for you.” At this Vivien looked at Merlin very strangely, and after a while she said, “Sir, if you would only share your wisdom and your cunning with me, then I believe I could love you very much. For, behold, I am only a young child in knowledge, and you are so old and so wise that I am afraid of you. If you would teach me your wisdom so that I might be your equal, then perhaps I could come to feel for you the regard that you wish me to feel.”

Merlin looked steadily at Vivien and said, “Damsel, you are certainly not the foolish child you claim to be. I can see that your eyes are bright with a cleverness far beyond your years. Now I doubt this: if I teach you the wisdom you want to have, it will either bring about your ruin or bring about mine.”
Then Vivien cried out in a loud, piercing voice, “Merlin, if you love me, teach me your wisdom and the cleverness of your magic! Then I will love you more than anyone else in all the world!”
But Merlin sighed deeply, for his heart was full of doubt. After a while he said, “Vivien, you shall have your way. I will teach you all the things of wisdom and magic that you wish to know.”

At this, Vivien was filled with such a fierce, painful joy that she did not dare let Merlin look at her face, for fear he would read what was written there. So she lowered her eyes and turned her face away from him. Then, after a little while, she said, “Master, when will you teach me that wisdom?”

Merlin answered, “I will not teach you today, or tomorrow, or in this place. I can only teach you such knowledge in a lonely spot, where nothing will disturb your studies. But tomorrow you must tell King Arthur that you need to return to your father’s kingdom. Then we will set out together with your attendants. When we have come to some hidden place, I will build a dwelling there by my magic, and we will stay in it until I have taught you wisdom.”
Then Vivien was overjoyed. She caught Merlin’s hand in hers and kissed it with great passion.

So the next day Vivien begged King Arthur to give her leave to return to her father’s Court. On the third day she and Merlin and a number of attendants who served the damsel left the Court of King Arthur. They rode out as though they were going to the Kingdom of Northumberland.

But when they had gone a little way from the King’s Court, they turned eastward and took the road toward a certain valley that Merlin knew. It was so fair and pleasant a place that it was sometimes called the Valley of Delight and sometimes the Valley of Joyousness.
